co_anti_gravity_wall_the.blurb: A small bouldering wall in the Red Cliff valley near Minturn and Vail, at roughly 8,700 feet. It is the first stone you meet after crossing the creek on the way to the rest of the garden, and it holds 15 problems on gneiss. The grades stay friendly: mostly V1 and V2, a V0 at the bottom, and a handful of V3 and V4 lines at the top end. The garden as a whole is shady, so it suits warmer days, and many problems around it are tall, so bring a few pads and a spotter. Early in spring, high water can make the crossing awkward.

co_murphy_s_dome_south_face.blurb: A south-facing granite face in the Deckers part of the South Platte, near 6,400 feet. Its 15 routes are mainly single pitches that depend on friction and balance rather than holds: ten sport lines, four trad and one top rope. Grades start around 5.6 and climb through the 5.9s and 5.10s, with a few in the 5.11s and one 5.12, so there is something for mid-grade climbers and a little for stronger ones. Bolts are on the newer side and anchors are two-bolt. Facing south, it can bake in summer, which makes spring, fall and mild winter days the better bet. The face is hidden from the north side, so finding the start takes some patience.

co_diamond_boulder.blurb: The largest and most convenient boulder on the east end of Riggs' Hill, on the edge of Grand Junction. It holds 15 problems across a wide range, from a very easy line and a few V1s up to a couple of V6s, with a good cluster between V3 and V5. The stone is generally solid with a little chipping. Pads are the only protection, and the block stands about fifteen feet at most. It sits a short walk uphill from the car, which makes it a quick after-work stop or a warm-up before moving to the neighbouring blocks.
co_diamond_boulder.parking_note: Use the small lot on the north side of South Broadway at the east end of Riggs' Hill. The boulder is a short walk straight up from there and easy to spot.

co_in_rainbows_boulder_area.blurb: A cluster of granite boulders on the hillside above the Da Butts trail near Buffalo Creek, in the South Platte, around 7,400 feet. There are 15 problems with a wide spread: a few easy lines, a middle group around V3 and V4, and a hard tail that climbs well into double-digit V grades. The namesake line, In Rainbows, is the area's headline at V4 and is tucked behind a larger boulder, so it takes a moment to find. Nearby blocks add shorter variations and a harder neighbor. Expect a quiet, cairn-marked walk rather than a roadside cragging scene.

co_middle_fork.blurb: A remote winter ice zone in the Cimarron Mountains south of Montrose, up the Middle Fork of the Cimarron River past Silver Jack Reservoir at about 10,000 feet. It holds 15 ice routes: six around WI3, four at WI4 and five at WI5, including a two-pitch WI5 line that is the area's most praised. A few climbs only come into shape late in the winter. Solitude is the draw, since routes can sit untouched for seasons. Reaching it in winter means a long drive on a plowed road that needs a capable vehicle, and heavy snow raises avalanche concerns.

co_devil_s_head_rock.blurb: A big granite face in the Devil's Head area of the Rampart Range, South Platte, facing southeast to south so it picks up sun early in the day. Its 15 routes are a mix of older trad lines and newer bolted sport climbs, from about 5.7 to the 5.11 range, with most in the 5.9 to 5.10 band. Many climbs are long multi-pitch outings, some running seven to ten pitches, so bring a 60 m rope (70 m helps) and a double rack to 4 inches for the crack lines. For its size it sees few climbers, which makes for a quiet day out on moderate terrain.

co_grendel_the.blurb: A steep, heavily featured crag high on a ridge in Golden Gate Canyon State Park, near Golden, at about 10,000 feet. The 15 routes are mostly bolted sport lines, with a few gear-protected ones, on west, southwest and southeast faces; the southwest face has the most. Grades run from about 5.8 up to 5.12, with the bulk in the 5.10 and 5.11 range. The wall looks larger from below than it proves to be, though several routes are long enough that a 70 m rope is worth carrying. The walk in is steep and takes most of an hour, which keeps the crag fairly quiet.

co_olympic_wall.blurb: A large, sunny granite wall on Independence Pass, at roughly 10,000 feet, and one of the more popular sections of the Outrageous Overhangs area. Its 15 routes are mostly bolted sport with a few trad options, and a small set of cams is handy where bolts are spaced for gear. Difficulty leans hard: most lines sit at 5.11 or 5.12, with one 5.13, plus a few 5.10s and easier warm-ups near 5.8. Climbs are steep, well crafted and frequently praised. The approach takes around twenty-five minutes, which helps thin out the crowds.
co_olympic_wall.parking_note: Leave the car at the Grotto Walls pullout on the pass road, then walk the highway shoulder to a small cairn on the left that marks the climbers' path.
co_olympic_wall.approach: From the Grotto Walls pullout, walk up the road a few hundred yards to a cairn on the left. A narrow trail climbs the bank, passing below Outrageous Overhangs, Thindependence and Junior Olympic Wall on the way to Opening Ceremony Wall. Olympic Wall is the big face immediately to its right.

_conflicts.co_diamond_boulder: Stored rock is shale; Riggs' Hill is described as covered in sandstone boulders (https://www.mountainproject.com/area/106253982/riggs-hill).
